{{Short description|Bounded linear operator}}
In [[mathematics]], in the area of [[functional analysis]] and [[operator theory]], the '''Volterra operator''', named after [[Vito Volterra]], is a [[bounded linear operator]] on the space ''L''<sup>2</sup>[0,1] of complex-valued [[square-integrable function]]s on the interval [0,1]. On the subspace ''C''[0,1] of [[continuous function]]s it represents [[indefinite integration]]. It is the operator corresponding to the [[Volterra integral equation]]s.

==Definition==
The Volterra operator, ''V'', may be defined for a function ''f''&nbsp;∈&nbsp;''L''<sup>2</sup>[0,1] and a value ''t''&nbsp;∈&nbsp;[0,1], as<ref>
{{cite book
| last1 = Rynne
| first1 = Bryan P.
| last2 = Youngson
| first2 = Martin A.
| title = Linear Functional Analysis
| publisher = Springer
| year = 2008
| chapter = Integral and Differential Equations 8.2. Volterra Integral Equations
| pages = 245
}}
</ref>

:<math>V(f)(t) = \int_{0}^{t} f(s)\, ds.</math>

==Properties==
*''V'' is a bounded linear operator between [[Hilbert space]]s, with kernel form<math display="block">Vf(x) = \int_0^1 1_{y \leq x} f(y) dy</math> proven by [[Fubini's theorem|exchanging the integral sign]].
*''V'' is a [[Hilbert–Schmidt operator]] with norm <math>\|V\|_{HS}^2 = 1/2</math>, hence in particular is [[compact operator|compact]].
*Its [[Hermitian adjoint]] has kernel form<math display="block">V^*(f)(x) = \int_{x}^{1} f(y)dy = \int_0^1 1_{y \geq x} f(y)dy</math>
*The positive-definite integral operator <math>K := V^* V</math> has kernel form<math display="block">Kf(x) = \int_0^1 \min(1-x, 1-y) f(y) dy</math>proven by exchanging the integral sign. Similarly, <math>VV^*</math> has kernel <math>\min(x, y)</math>. They are [[Self-adjoint operator|unitarily equivalent]] via <math>Uf(x) = f(1-x)</math>, so both have the same spectrum.
*The eigenfunctions of <math>VV^*</math> satisfy <math>\begin{cases}
f(1) &= 0 \\
f'(0) &= 0 \\
f''(x) &= -\lambda^{-1} f
\end{cases}</math> with solution <math display="block">f(x) = \sin((k+1/2) \pi x), \lambda = \left(\frac{1}{(k+ 1/2) \pi}\right)^2</math>with <math>k = 0, 1, 2, \dots</math>.
*The [[Singular value|singular values]] of ''V'' are <math>((k + 1/2) \pi)^{-1}</math> with <math>k = 0, 1, 2, \dots</math>.
*The [[operator norm]] of ''V'' is <math>2/\pi</math>.
*''V'' is not [[trace class]].
*''V'' has no [[eigenvalue]]s and therefore, by the [[spectral theory of compact operators]], its [[spectrum (functional analysis)|spectrum]] ''σ''(''V'') = {0}.<ref name="stackexchange_indefinite-integrators">{{cite web |date=May 30, 2012 |title=Spectrum of Indefinite Integral Operators |url=https://math.stackexchange.com/q/151425 |work=[[Stack Exchange]]}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Volterra Operator is compact but has no eigenvalue |work=[[Stack Exchange]] |url=https://math.stackexchange.com/q/219699}}</ref>
*''V'' is a [[quasinilpotent operator]] (that is, the [[spectral radius]], ''ρ''(''V''), is zero), but it is not [[nilpotent operator]].
